items.title: Show HN: Robin – Non-algorithmic Twitter client
items.summary: Information pollution affects all of us. When we are served a random mix of important news, half-truths and “For You” posts from strangers in the same feed, our ability to make sense of the world are diminished. Over time, it wears us down. Robin is an open source Twitter/X client for iOS and Android. It restores a clean, chronological set of posts (only from people you follow.) You can hide posts using keywords (e.g. noisy politicians' names.) It also lets you fact-check claims quickly by long-pressing on the post. Our goal is simple – Lower the amount of distractions and the unwanted stress caused by hot takes and replies from random people we don’t know nor care about. Launch post: https://evergreen-labs.org/blog/introducing-robin iOS: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/robin-non-algorithmic-x/id6817... Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.evergreenl... Public Repo: https://github.com/billylo1/Robin

items.title: Show HN: Amgi – Plain-text spaced repetition with FSRS
items.summary: Hi HN! I love Anki and I've been using it for 5–6 months pretty much consistently. It's a wonderful piece of software, but its obvious downside is its UI. I love beautiful things, and spending 30–40 minutes daily on something that doesn't bring me aesthetic joy is kinda urgh... So I'm building Amgi (암기, means memorization in Korean), an open-source plain-text spaced repetition system with FSRS. I started building it only a week ago. Flash cards are simply Markdown files with pretty elegant syntax, so you are not tied to any app. Just open your flashcards folder in your favorite editor and add/edit straightaway: Q: What does FSRS stand for? A: Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler C: The capital of [France] is [Paris|city]. Amgi has a dashboard where you can see your streak & some statistics on your reviews, and a browser where you can search using queries similar to Anki's (deck:Name, #tag, is:due, etc.). It also supports LaTeX, images, audio and code blocks (incl. making cloze cards inside of them). And it has a cute installer! (I hope) It can already import from Anki, but it's still pretty early and the only Anki collection I've tested on is my own, so expect some rough edges. Mac-only for now! My own collection is public too, it's the actual one I use daily: https://github.com/alisheryeginbay/flashcards Would love feedback, especially on the card syntax :)

items.summary: I first tried to play Megabonk on my Mac with Wine 11.0 and DXMT 0.80. After successfully playing it, I thought it would be great to make a packaged app - a one-click installer - so non-developer users can also easily play Windows Steam games on mac. Pear is a free, open-source macOS app that sets up a Windows Steam environment on Apple Silicon. It handles runtime setup and launching Steam. You sign in through Valve's Steam client, then install and play games you own. The current release is 0.1.1 and requires Apple Silicon, macOS 15 or later, and Rosetta. Only Megabonk has been tested. items.title: Show HN: CATT 0.2.1: Test agents/services against a Muse/Instinct-alike, in CI
items.summary: Hey HN, we recently open sourced our Consumer Agent Testing Tool to help teams iterate against proprietary assistants like Muse and Instinct. We built this to reduce our own frustrations with building an MCP/API for these agents to consume. The problem: testing against these tools is hard! Agent memory + account statefulness make reproducibility, in the ways required for repeatable/reliable outcomes, between agents and the APIs/MCPs they interact with very challenging. The solution: CATT lets devs test their services against a surrogate Muse or Instinct agent (not affiliated with either of these companies). Testers define starting conditions, approvals, and success conditions for their service's state. CATT then records the full interaction (incl. tool calls, responses) so it can diff what happened from what the agent reports. Runs can be tested in local builds or via CI, with or without LLM backing. CATT is designed to emulate the important parts of personal assistant interactions. Its got: - Tool calls and command-line tool access - Simulated approvals for service actions - Outcomes tracking and comparison - Optional MCP profile based on an unofficial Muse template There are limitations to how much we know about different assistant specific behaviors so the tool labels its assumptions as `documented`, `unofficial`, `assumed` or `unknown` for developer review. We'll do our best to keep the tool updated as new insights about the internal workings of these assistants come to light. It is an area of active research and interest, a good example is this recent report on how Instinct uses Exa for web search [0]. Are you building a connector or MCP? If yes, we'd like to hear from you! Have you had assistants behave incoherently, use stale information, or procalim success without evidence? What else should we add tests for? The best way to get started is...to point your coding assistant at the repo and ask it to integrate the tool with your CI or local testing pipeline! Hope it's helpful! [0]: https://www.sunbeam.ai/thoughts/instinct-is-using-exa-for-we...
